title: Carboxylic acid derivatives
goal: Substitution at C=O: addition, then elimination, and when a second nucleophile adds.

problemSets.title: Addition–elimination
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: The nucleophile adds to C=O, then the C=O re-forms and pushes out a leaving group.
problemSets.conceptCard:
Acid chlorides, anhydrides, esters and amides all have a **leaving group** on the carbonyl carbon. Substitution there is never SN2. It takes two steps:

1. **addition**: the nucleophile bonds to the carbonyl carbon and the C=O π pair moves onto oxygen, giving a *tetrahedral intermediate*
2. **elimination**: an oxygen lone pair re-forms C=O and the best leaving group goes

The better the leaving group, the more reactive the derivative: acid chloride > anhydride > ester > amide. In acid, protonate the C=O first and make sure every group leaves as a neutral molecule.

setItems.whyThisOne: The most reactive derivative: chloride leaves, a second amine takes the proton.
Hydroxide in, methoxide out; the last proton transfer makes it irreversible.
The same substitution in acid: every step reversible, every proton accounted for.

problemSets.title: Making esters and amides
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Turn OH into a good leaving group, or start from a derivative that already has one.
problemSets.conceptCard:
A carboxylic acid is a poor electrophile and OH⁻ a poor leaving group. Three ways round it:

- **acid catalysis**: protonate the C=O, and later the OH, so that *water* leaves (Fischer esterification)
- **a more reactive derivative**: an anhydride gives up acetate, a much better leaving group; a weak base such as pyridine mops up the proton
- **a coupling reagent**: DCC turns the OH into an *O-acylisourea*, a leaving group that departs as dicyclohexylurea

An amine and an acid on their own just make a salt: that is why amides need activation.

setItems.whyThisOne: Hydrolysis run backwards: excess methanol drives it to the ester.
Acetate leaves; pyridine is only the base.
DCC activates the acid so that an amine can attack.

problemSets.title: Two additions
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Strong nucleophiles add twice to an ester, because the ketone or aldehyde formed is more reactive.
problemSets.conceptCard:
Grignard reagents and LiAlH₄ add to an ester, and the tetrahedral intermediate loses alkoxide as usual. But the **ketone** or **aldehyde** formed is *more* electrophilic than the ester, so a second equivalent adds at once:

- Grignard reagent + ester → **tertiary alcohol** with two identical groups
- LiAlH₄ + ester → **primary alcohol**

DIBAL-H at −78 °C stops after one hydride: the tetrahedral intermediate, bound to aluminium, is stable until the work-up, when no hydride is left. The work-up then releases the **aldehyde**.

setItems.whyThisOne: Two methyl groups add; you cannot stop at the ketone.
Two hydrides: the ester becomes a primary alcohol.
One hydride at −78 °C; the work-up gives the aldehyde.

problemSets.title: Checkpoint
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Add, collapse, and decide which group leaves and whether a second nucleophile adds.
problemSets.conceptCard: Reactions from every set, shuffled, names hidden until you finish. Three attempts per step.

setItems.whyThisOne: A second addition and a work-up.
